library(SimplyAgree)

# Background

Reliability studies ask two related questions. *Relative* reliability asks
whether a measurement ranks subjects consistently; it is summarised by an
intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), the proportion of the observed
variance that is due to real differences between subjects. *Absolute*
reliability asks how much a single measurement varies around a subject's
true value; it is summarised by the standard error of measurement (SEM),
also called the typical error [@hopkins2000], often expressed as a
coefficient of variation. The calculations here follow @weir2005, who in
turn relies on @shrout1979 and @mcgraw1996.

`SimplyAgree` has one function for each question, each returning a standard
`htest` object with a confidence interval and, optionally, a test:

| Function | Estimates |
|---|---|
| `icc_test()` | One ICC |
| `reli_err_test()` | The SEM, SEE or SEP, in units, sympercents or % of the mean |
| `mdc_test()` | The minimal detectable change (MDC) |
| `power_icc()`, `precision_icc()` | Sample size for an ICC study |

The older `reli_stats()` and `reli_aov()`, which return everything at once,
are superseded (see [Legacy functions](#legacy-functions)).

All functions accept data in three ways: a formula, `values ~ item | id`;
long data, with `measure`, `item` and `id` column names; or wide data, one
row per subject, with the item columns in `col.names`. An *item* is
whatever is repeated: a trial, an occasion, a rater, or a judge.

As an example, take the data of @shrout1979 (6 subjects rated by 4 judges).

```{r}
dat <- data.frame(judge1 = c(9, 6, 8, 7, 10, 6),
                  judge2 = c(2, 1, 4, 1, 5, 2),
                  judge3 = c(5, 3, 6, 2, 6, 4),
                  judge4 = c(8, 2, 8, 6, 9, 7))
judges <- c("judge1", "judge2", "judge3", "judge4")
```

# The intraclass correlation coefficient

```{r}
icc_test(col.names = judges, data = dat)
```

## Choosing the ICC

The form is set by three arguments, each answering one question about the
study and how its results will be used. Answer them in order.

1. **Is every subject measured by the same items** (the same trials,
   raters, or devices)? Yes: `model = "twoway"`. No, each subject is
   measured by different items (for example, raters drawn from a pool):
   `model = "oneway"`, which only has an absolute-agreement form.
2. **Should systematic differences between items count as error?**
   Yes, `type = "agreement"`, when measurements from different items will be
   used interchangeably or on their absolute values: any rater's score is
   taken as it is, scores are compared with a fixed cut-off, or sessions are
   pooled. No, `type = "consistency"`, when only the subjects' relative
   standing matters, or when systematic differences (a learning or fatigue
   effect, a rater who scores high) are checked and reported separately.
3. **Will a single measurement or the mean of k be used in practice?**
   One measurement: `unit = "single"`. The mean of the same k items as in
   the study: `unit = "average"`.

Some common designs:

| Study | ICC | Arguments | Matching error statistic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Test-retest, trial effects checked separately [@hopkins2000; @weir2005] | ICC(C,1) | defaults | `reli_err_test()` (\(\sqrt{MS_E}\)) |
| Test-retest, absolute values used (e.g. compared with a threshold) | ICC(A,1) | `type = "agreement"` | `reli_err_test(type = "agreement")` |
| Inter-rater, the same raters rate every subject, scores used interchangeably | ICC(A,1) | `type = "agreement"` | `reli_err_test(type = "agreement")` |
| Inter-rater, the same raters, only rank order matters | ICC(C,1) | defaults | `reli_err_test()` |
| Each subject rated by different raters | ICC(1) | `model = "oneway"` | `reli_err_test(model = "oneway")` |
| The score used in practice is the mean of the k ratings or trials | ICC(C,k), ICC(A,k), ICC(k) | `unit = "average"` | — |
| Two methods measuring the same quantity (method comparison) | — | `agreement_limit()`, `ccc_test()` | limits of agreement |

Whether the items are thought of as fixed (these particular raters) or
random (a sample of possible raters) changes how widely the result
generalises, not how it is calculated [@mcgraw1996]. The average-measure
forms describe the mean of the k items in this study; other values of k
would need a Spearman-Brown projection. Whatever the form, report the
matching error statistic, and test against a meaningful threshold rather
than labelling the estimate "good" or "poor".

The three arguments map onto the names used by @mcgraw1996 and
@shrout1979:

| `model` | `type` | `unit` | McGraw & Wong | Shrout & Fleiss |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| oneway | agreement | single | ICC(1) | ICC(1,1) |
| oneway | agreement | average | ICC(k) | ICC(1,k) |
| twoway | agreement | single | ICC(A,1) | ICC(2,1) |
| twoway | agreement | average | ICC(A,k) | ICC(2,k) |
| twoway | consistency | single | ICC(C,1) | ICC(3,1) |
| twoway | consistency | average | ICC(C,k) | ICC(3,k) |

The default, ICC(C,1), follows @hopkins2000 and @weir2005: check for
systematic change between trials separately (for example with
`t.test()` for two trials), then report the consistency ICC, which is tied
to the SEM. Others, such as @koo2016, recommend absolute agreement for
test-retest studies:

```{r}
icc_test(col.names = judges, data = dat, type = "agreement")
```

## Related coefficients: Cronbach's alpha and the CCC

Two other widely used coefficients are ICCs in disguise.

**Cronbach's alpha is ICC(C,k).** With complete data, Cronbach's
[-@cronbach1951] alpha for k items equals the average-measure consistency
ICC, \((MS_B - MS_E)/MS_B\) [@mcgraw1996]. So alpha is the reliability of
the *mean* (or sum) of the k items when systematic differences between
items do not count, not the reliability of a single item; ICC(C,1) is the
corresponding single-item figure. Here alpha computed from its usual
formula matches `icc_test(unit = "average")`:

```{r}
k <- length(judges)
alpha <- k / (k - 1) * (1 - sum(apply(dat, 2, var)) / var(rowSums(dat)))
c(alpha = alpha,
  icc_C_k = unname(icc_test(col.names = judges, data = dat,
                            unit = "average")$estimate))
```

**The CCC is close to ICC(A,1) for two methods.** Lin's concordance
correlation coefficient [@Lin1989] measures how closely pairs fall on the
line of identity, so systematic differences between the methods count as
disagreement, as in an absolute-agreement ICC. For two methods it is
essentially ICC(A,1): the estimators differ only in using n rather than
n - 1 in the variances, and the difference vanishes as n grows
[@nickerson1997; @carrasco2003]. The two answer different questions in
practice: `ccc_test()` is meant for comparing two methods (alongside
limits of agreement), `icc_test()` for the reliability of a measurement
across trials or raters.

```{r}
two <- dat[c("judge1", "judge4")]
c(CCC = unname(ccc_test(x = "judge1", y = "judge4", data = two)$estimate),
  ICC_A_1 = unname(icc_test(col.names = c("judge1", "judge4"), data = two,
                            type = "agreement")$estimate))
```

With only 6 subjects the n versus n - 1 difference is visible; with a few
dozen subjects the two estimates agree to about two decimal places.

## Testing against a threshold

By default no test is done: testing whether an ICC differs from 0 is rarely
informative. No qualitative labels ("good", "excellent") are given either,
because published cutoffs disagree and the ICC depends on how much subjects
differ from each other [@weir2005]. To claim that reliability exceeds a
value, test against it:

```{r}
res <- icc_test(col.names = judges, data = dat,
                null.value = 0.5, alternative = "greater")
res
```

With a one-sided alternative the interval is one-sided too: its lower limit
is the one-sided bound that matches the test.

## Describing the result

`summary()` describes the result in words, in one of two styles. With a
test, the default is the usual decision about the null hypothesis:

```{r}
summary(res)
```

The estimation style, following @greenland2019 and @rafi2020, describes the
interval as a range of values compatible with the data and converts the
p-value to an S-value, \(s = -\log_2 p\): the bits of information against
the tested hypothesis, as surprising as \(s\) heads in a row from a fair
coin.

```{r}
summary(res, style = "estimation")
```

## Missing data

`method = "anova"` (the default) needs every subject measured on every
item. With missing measurements, `method = "reml"` fits a linear mixed
model; its intervals use degrees of freedom based on the observed data and
are approximate, so a warning is given.

```{r}
dat_na <- dat
dat_na$judge2[1] <- NA
icc_test(col.names = judges, data = dat_na, method = "reml")
```

## Bootstrap intervals and standard errors

**When to bootstrap.** The F-based intervals assume normal data. In
simulations (3 trials, 10 or 30 subjects, ICC 0.5 or 0.9), they covered
0.92 to 0.97 of the time with normal data but only 0.80 to 0.93 with skewed
or heavy-tailed data. With `boot = TRUE`, the interval comes from a
nonparametric bootstrap instead, which helps with clearly non-normal data
and about 30 or more subjects. With 10 subjects every method, the bootstrap
included, falls short of its nominal coverage, so a bootstrap is no cure
for a small sample.

**How it works.** Each replicate resamples subjects with replacement,
keeping all of each subject's measurements, and refits the model
(`replicates` times, 1999 by default; with `method = "reml"` this means
refitting the mixed model each time, which is slow). The interval type is
set by `boot_ci`; the default, `"auto"`, picks the type that did best in the
simulations:

| Estimate | `method = "anova"` | `method = "reml"` |
|---|---|---|
| ICC (`icc_test()`) | studentized | percentile |
| SEM, SEE, SEP, consistency or one-way (`reli_err_test()`) | studentized | percentile |
| SEM, SEP, two-way agreement (`reli_err_test()`) | BCa | percentile |

Any p-value comes from inverting the bootstrap interval, so it is
approximate and always agrees with the interval.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
icc_test(col.names = judges, data = dat, boot = TRUE, replicates = 499)
```

**The hybrid step for agreement.** Resampling subjects keeps the same items
(judges, trials) in every replicate, so on its own it treats the items as
fixed. An absolute-agreement ICC (and the agreement SEM and SEP) treats the
items as a sample, and their systematic differences count as error, so
plain subject resampling misses the uncertainty that comes from which items
happened to be used. In simulations it covered only 0.70 to 0.80 for an
agreement ICC of 0.9. Each replicate therefore also multiplies the item mean
square by an independent \(\chi^2_{k-1}/(k-1)\) draw, its sampling variation
under normal theory. This "hybrid" bootstrap restored coverage to about
0.94 to 0.96 with normal data and 30 subjects. It is applied automatically to
the two-way agreement forms; when the items really are fixed it is somewhat
conservative, like the F interval.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
icc_test(col.names = judges, data = dat, type = "agreement", boot = TRUE,
         replicates = 499)
```

**Standard errors (`se_method`).** Every result reports standard errors in
`stderr`, and the studentized bootstrap divides each replicate by its own
standard error. Three estimates are available:

- `"jackknife"` (default): delete one subject at a time. It averaged 0.89 to
  1.08 times the true sampling SD in simulations, including skewed data and
  missing measurements. It is cheap with complete data and needs n refits
  with `method = "reml"`.
- `"influence"`: a sandwich estimate from each subject's influence. It is
  cheap everywhere but too small with few subjects (0.69 to 1.00 times the
  true SD), and it is the only option for the studentized bootstrap with
  `method = "reml"`.
- `"normal"`: normal theory. It is accurate with normal data (0.87 to 1.04)
  but too small with skewed or heavy-tailed data (0.60 to 0.80). It depends
  only on the degrees of freedom, so it cannot be used to studentize.

`se_method` changes `stderr` and the studentized bootstrap, never the
F-based (or chi-square) interval and test.

```{r}
res_j <- icc_test(col.names = judges, data = dat)
res_n <- icc_test(col.names = judges, data = dat, se_method = "normal")
rbind(jackknife = res_j$stderr, normal = res_n$stderr)
```

More detail, including the full simulation results, is in `?icc_test` and
`?reli_err_test`.

## Plots and diagnostics

`plot()` shows each subject's measurements across the items (grey), with
the item means and their 95% confidence intervals (blue), so systematic
differences between items stand out against the spread of subjects.

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=4}
res <- icc_test(col.names = judges, data = dat)
plot(res)
```

Other views are chosen with `type`: `"subjects"` orders the subjects by
their mean and shows each subject's measurements, which compares the spread
between subjects with the scatter within subjects (what the ICC
summarises); `"items"` shows each measurement's deviation from its
subject's mean by item (systematic item differences, which count as error
for an agreement ICC but not for a consistency ICC); and `"pairs"` plots each
pair of items against each other with the line of identity.

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=4}
plot(res, type = "subjects")
```

`check()` gives model diagnostics: the normality and homogeneity of the
residuals, and the within-subject SD against the subject mean. An SD that
rises with the mean means the error grows with the size of the measurement,
and a coefficient of variation (`reli_err_test(scale = "log")`, below)
describes it better than an error in units.

```{r, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.5}
check(res)
```

# Measurement error

`reli_err_test()` estimates the standard error of measurement (SEM),
estimate (SEE) or prediction (SEP). With the defaults it gives the typical
error: \(\sqrt{MS_E}\) from the two-way analysis of variance, which excludes
systematic differences between trials. As an example, take data set A of
@weir2005 (8 subjects, 2 trials).

```{r}
weir <- data.frame(t1 = c(146, 148, 170, 90, 157, 156, 176, 205),
                   t2 = c(140, 152, 152, 99, 145, 153, 167, 218))
reli_err_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir)
```

To show that the error is smaller than an acceptable value, give it as
`null.value` (the default alternative is `"less"`):

```{r}
reli_err_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, null.value = 12)
```

The SEE is the standard error of a subject's estimated true score, and the
SEP is used to judge whether a change from the estimated true score is
real [@weir2005]. Both depend on the ICC and on how much subjects differ,
so the SEM is the better general description of measurement error.

```{r}
reli_err_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, stat = "SEP")
```

The SEE and SEP use the SD matched to the ICC's denominator (for the
consistency ICC, \(SD^2 = \sigma^2_{subjects} + \sigma^2_{error}\)), so that
\(SD\sqrt{1 - ICC}\) equals the SEM exactly. @weir2005 uses the SD of all
the measurements instead, so his SEE and SEP (7.1 and 10.2 here) are
slightly smaller than these (7.35 and 10.54).

# Coefficient of variation

When the error grows with the size of the measurements, it is better
expressed relative to them [@atkinson1998; @hopkins2000]. `reli_err_test()`
gives the coefficient of variation in two ways.

`scale = "log"` analyses the log-transformed measurements and reports
100 times the statistic, in sympercents [@cole2000]. The SEM keeps its exact
interval.

```{r}
reli_err_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, scale = "log")
```

A sympercent \(s\) converts to the conventional CV% as
\(100\sqrt{\exp((s/100)^2) - 1}\); below about 15% the two are nearly
identical (10 sympercents is a CV of 10.03%). The conversion is monotone, so
it can be applied to the interval limits too.

`scale = "mean"` divides the statistic by the grand mean (the "pooled" CV);
its interval allows for the uncertainty in the mean.

```{r}
reli_err_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, scale = "mean")
```

In both cases `null.value` is on the same scale as the estimate.

# MDC, SDD and the repeatability coefficient

The minimal detectable change (MDC), smallest detectable or real difference
(SDD, SRD), "minimal difference" [@weir2005] and repeatability coefficient
are all the SEM scaled by \(z \sqrt{2}\): for 95%,
\(1.96 \sqrt{2} \times SEM\), the change between two measurements of one
subject that measurement error alone would exceed only 5% of the time.
`mdc_test()` computes it, with an interval (the SEM interval, scaled):

```{r}
mdc_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir)
```

`sided = "one.sided"` gives the MDC for a change in one stated direction,
`k_avg` the MDC for scores that are means of several trials, and
`scale = "log"` the MDC as a percentage (in `percent`, as an increase and a
decrease). An existing SEM can be reused without refitting, as
`mdc_test(sem)`. With two trials the MDC is the half-width of the limits of
agreement of `agreement_limit()`, which also reports the bias between
trials. @weir2005 notes that, strictly, real change should be judged against
an interval around the subject's estimated true score, using the SEP.

**Differences between raters.** The MDC also answers a common inter-rater
question: how far apart could two raters' (or devices') measurements of the
same subject be? Each measurement has error SEM, so their difference has
error SD \(\sqrt{2} \times SEM\), the same reasoning as for two occasions.
When the raters are interchangeable (any rater's score is used as it is, and
the raters are thought of as drawn from a pool), use the agreement SEM, so
that systematic differences between raters count as error:

```{r}
mdc_test(col.names = judges, data = dat, type = "agreement")
```

Two of the judges differing by less than this would be consistent with
measurement error alone. The consistency SEM would leave out the judges'
systematic differences, which are large here, and give an MDC of only
about 2.8. For two particular raters,
`agreement_limit()` reports their bias and the spread around it separately.
The SEP is not the statistic for this: it concerns a change from a subject's
estimated true score, and \(1.96 \times SEP\) does not bound the difference
between two raters.

**What the MDC is not.** The MDC is a threshold for *one individual's*
change. It is not a threshold for an average (group) effect: the
uncertainty of a mean change shrinks with the number of subjects, so a mean
effect well below the MDC can be estimated precisely and be clearly
different from zero. An effect smaller than the MDC is small relative to one
person's measurement noise; that does not make it noise. The MDC
should never be used to count "responders". An observed change mixes the true response
with within-person variation, so even if everyone responded identically,
some would exceed the MDC and some would not [@senn2004]. Real differences
in response need a control group or replicated crossover designs
[@atkinson2015; @senn2016].

**The MDC and a change that matters.** The MDC describes noise; whether a
change *matters* needs an external anchor, such as a clinically important
difference. Give it as `null.value` to test whether the MDC is below it,
i.e. whether such a change can be told apart from measurement error:

```{r}
mdc_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, null.value = 30)
```

A "smallest worthwhile change" (SWC) computed from the same reliability
data is not such an anchor. With 0.2 times the between-subject SD
[@hopkins2004], its ratio to the SEM is \(0.2/\sqrt{1 - ICC}\), a
restatement of the ICC. @hopkins2004 offers it as a default (e.g. for
fitness tests in team sports) when no relationship to a real outcome is
available, and it should be treated as such a fallback.

## Hopkins's smallest worthwhile change (SWC)

I want give a quick example of Hopkin's SWC here because this quick example and thought experiment was enlightening for me. @hopkins2004 defined the SWC as 0.3 times the CV of top
athletes' performance from one *competition* to the next. Because of that
race-to-race variation (let's assume track athletes here), evenly matched athletes take turns winning;
simulations showed that an enhancement of 0.3 of the CV gives a top athlete
about one extra win in 10 events [@hopkins1999]. The CV comes from
competitions, not from the test, so it is an external anchor. The test's own
typical error must not be used in its place. To be clear here, 0.3 times the CV (from SEM) is a fixed 11% of
the MDC for every test (\(0.3 / (1.96\sqrt{2}) \approx 0.11\)), so it says
nothing about whether a change matters for competition.

The competition CV is a typical error with competitions in place of trials,
so `reli_err_test()` estimates it from repeated competition results. A few
choices matter:

- **Top athletes only.** Less successful athletes may vary more from race to
  race, so including the whole field makes the SWC too large. So, I'd be careful about who you include.
- **The consistency SEM (the default).** Course, weather and tactics shift
  everyone in a race together, and placings depend on performance relative
  to the field; the two-way consistency SEM removes those shifts.
  `type = "agreement"` would count them as athlete variability.
- **`method = "reml"`**, because athletes rarely compete in every event.
- **`scale = "log"`**, as Hopkins does, so the CV is in sympercents.
- **A short span**, such as one season, so that long-term trends in an
  athlete's performance are not counted as noise.
- **The same measure as the test.** A CV for race time is not a CV for
  power; @hopkins2004 suggests multiplying a time CV by about 2 to 3 for
  mean power (i.e., applying it to the test-retest data).

Simulated results for 15 top athletes over 8 races in a season (times in
seconds), with a within-athlete CV of 1% and some races missed:

```{r}
set.seed(2004)
races <- expand.grid(athlete = paste0("A", 1:15), race = paste0("R", 1:8))
ability <- rnorm(15, 0, 0.01)  # differences between athletes
course <- rnorm(8, 0, 0.02)    # race conditions shift everyone
races$time <- 240 * exp(ability[races$athlete] + course[races$race] +
                          rnorm(nrow(races), 0, 0.01))
races <- races[runif(nrow(races)) > 0.2, ]  # missed races

cv_comp <- reli_err_test(time ~ race | athlete, data = races,
                         scale = "log", method = "reml")
cv_comp
swc <- 0.3 * unname(cv_comp$estimate)
swc
```

A test can then be judged against the SWC in two ways; here, a simulated
laboratory time trial with 12 athletes and 2 trials. Hopkins's criterion is
that the noise is smaller than the signal: the test's typical error below
the SWC. That is the test of the SEM against `null.value = swc`:

```{r}
lab <- data.frame(id = rep(paste0("S", 1:12), 2),
                  trial = rep(c("t1", "t2"), each = 12))
lab$time <- 300 * exp(rep(rnorm(12, 0, 0.02), 2) + rnorm(24, 0, 0.008))
lab_sem <- reli_err_test(time ~ trial | id, data = lab, scale = "log",
                         null.value = swc)
lab_sem
```

The stricter question, whether one athlete's change the size of the SWC can
be told apart from measurement error with 95% confidence, is the MDC against
the same value:

```{r}
lab_mdc <- mdc_test(lab_sem, null.value = swc)
lab_mdc
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
te <- unname(lab_sem$estimate)
swc_ci <- 0.3 * as.numeric(cv_comp$conf.int)
```

Here the time trial's typical error (`r sprintf("%.2f", te)`%) is
`r round(te / swc, 1)` times the SWC (`r sprintf("%.2f", swc)`%), and its MDC
(`r round(unname(lab_mdc$estimate), 1)`%) is
`r round(unname(lab_mdc$estimate) / swc)` times it. That is common
[@hopkins2004]: a change of SWC size in one athlete cannot be distinguished
from noise with this test. Averaging \(k\) trials (`k_avg`) shrinks the
error by \(\sqrt{k}\), but bringing it down to the SWC would take about
`r ceiling((te / swc)^2)` trials. The SWC is itself an estimate (0.3 times
the interval for the CV gives `r sprintf("%.2f", swc_ci[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", swc_ci[2])`), and using it as `null.value` treats it as known.

# Planning a reliability study

`power_icc()` gives the power of the ICC test, or the number of subjects
(`n`), measurements per subject (`k`), or the ICC under the alternative
needed for a given power. For example, the subjects needed to show, with
two trials and 80% power, that the ICC is above 0.6 when it is really 0.8:

```{r}
power_icc(rho0 = 0.6, rho1 = 0.8, k = 2, power = 0.8,
          alternative = "greater")
```

`precision_icc()` instead plans for a narrow confidence interval: here, the
subjects needed for a 95% interval no wider than 0.2 around an ICC of 0.8,
with three trials, with 80% assurance (the probability that the interval is
that narrow).

```{r}
precision_icc(rho = 0.8, k = 3, width = 0.2, assurance = 0.8)
```

Both are exact for the one-way and consistency ICCs; `method =
"approximate"` reproduces the published formulas of @walter1998 and
@zou2012 (see also @mondal2024). The agreement ICC has no exact
distribution and is not supported. See
`vignette("power_sample_size_vignette", package = "SimplyAgree")` for more
examples, including average measures, missing measurements, and how to use
these calculations as a guide for agreement ICCs.

# Legacy functions

`reli_stats()` (linear mixed model) and `reli_aov()` (analysis of variance)
return all six ICCs, the CV, SEM, SEE and SEP at once. They are superseded
but still work.

```{r}
reli_aov(data = dat, wide = TRUE, col.names = judges)
```

Since version 0.4.0 they use the same engine as `icc_test()`. In
particular, their ICC intervals are now two-sided. Previous versions used
`conf.level` in each tail, so a "95%" interval was really a 90% interval;
the old numbers at `conf.level = c` are reproduced with
`conf.level = 1 - 2 * (1 - c)`. Their SEE and SEP keep the SD of all the
measurements, as in @weir2005. See `?reli_stats` for the other changes.

# Calculative approach

## Model and mean squares

For n subjects each measured on k items, the two-way model is
\(y_{ij} = \mu + s_i + t_j + e_{ij}\), with subject effects \(s_i\)
(variance \(\sigma^2_s\)), item effects \(t_j\) (\(\sigma^2_t\)) and error
\(e_{ij}\) (\(\sigma^2_e\)). The analysis of variance gives the mean squares
for subjects (\(MS_B\), \(n - 1\) df), items (\(MS_J\), \(k - 1\) df) and
error (\(MS_E\), \((n-1)(k-1)\) df), and the within-subject mean square
\(MS_W = (MS_J + (n-1) MS_E)/n\) (\(n(k-1)\) df). Their expectations are

$$
E(MS_B) = k\sigma^2_s + \sigma^2_e, \quad
E(MS_J) = n\sigma^2_t + \sigma^2_e, \quad
E(MS_E) = \sigma^2_e.
$$

With `method = "reml"`, the variance components come from a linear mixed
model and the mean squares are reconstructed from them.

## Intraclass correlation coefficients

$$
ICC(1) = \frac{MS_B - MS_W}{MS_B + (k-1) MS_W}
$$

$$
ICC(A,1) = \frac{MS_B - MS_E}{MS_B + (k-1) MS_E + k (MS_J - MS_E)/n}
$$

$$
ICC(C,1) = \frac{MS_B - MS_E}{MS_B + (k-1) MS_E}
$$

The average-measure forms are the Spearman-Brown projection of the
single-measure form to k items, \(k\rho / (1 + (k-1)\rho)\); for example
\(ICC(C,k) = (MS_B - MS_E)/MS_B\) and
\(ICC(A,k) = (MS_B - MS_E)/(MS_B + (MS_J - MS_E)/n)\).

## Confidence intervals and tests

A two-sided \(1 - \alpha\) interval uses \(\alpha/2\) in each tail
[@shrout1979; @mcgraw1996]. For ICC(1) and ICC(C,1), with
\(F = MS_B/MS_W\) or \(MS_B/MS_E\) and its degrees of freedom
\((\nu_1, \nu_2)\),

$$
F_L = \frac{F}{F_{1-\alpha/2;\, \nu_1, \nu_2}}, \quad
F_U = F \cdot F_{1-\alpha/2;\, \nu_2, \nu_1}, \quad
\text{limits} = \frac{F_{L,U} - 1}{F_{L,U} + k - 1}.
$$

These intervals are exact. For ICC(A,1) the denominator degrees of freedom
are approximated [@satterthwaite1946; @mcgraw1996],

$$
v = \frac{(a MS_J + b MS_E)^2}{\frac{(a MS_J)^2}{k-1} +
\frac{(b MS_E)^2}{(n-1)(k-1)}}, \quad
a = \frac{k \hat\rho}{n(1-\hat\rho)}, \quad
b = 1 + \frac{k\hat\rho (n-1)}{n(1-\hat\rho)},
$$

and with \(F^*_{L} = F_{1-\alpha/2;\, n-1, v}\) and
\(F^*_{U} = F_{1-\alpha/2;\, v, n-1}\),

$$
L = \frac{n(MS_B - F^*_L MS_E)}{F^*_L (k MS_J + (kn - k - n) MS_E) + n MS_B},
\quad
U = \frac{n(F^*_U MS_B - MS_E)}{k MS_J + (kn - k - n) MS_E + n F^*_U MS_B}.
$$

The tests of \(H_0: \rho = \rho_0\) are the F tests of @mcgraw1996: for
ICC(C,1), \(F = (MS_B/MS_E)(1-\rho_0)/(1 + (k-1)\rho_0)\) on
\((n-1, (n-1)(k-1))\) degrees of freedom, and similarly for the other forms.

## Standard errors of measurement

| Statistic | Estimate | Interval |
|---|---|---|
| SEM, two-way consistency | \(\sqrt{MS_E}\) | exact \(\chi^2\) |
| SEM, two-way agreement | \(\sqrt{(MS_J + (n-1)MS_E)/n}\) | Satterthwaite \(\chi^2\) |
| SEM, one-way | \(\sqrt{MS_W}\) | exact \(\chi^2\) |
| SEE | \(SD\sqrt{ICC(1-ICC)}\) | delta method, log scale |
| SEP | \(SD\sqrt{1-ICC^2}\) | delta method, log scale |

For example, the exact interval for the consistency SEM is
\(\sqrt{\nu MS_E / \chi^2_{1-\alpha/2;\,\nu}}\) to
\(\sqrt{\nu MS_E / \chi^2_{\alpha/2;\,\nu}}\) with \(\nu = (n-1)(k-1)\).

# Inter-Rater Reliability

The ICC is for continuous measurements. For categorical or ordinal ratings
(a diagnosis, a grade, a severity scale), agreement between raters is
summarised instead by chance-corrected agreement coefficients such as Gwet's
AC1, Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha (`cac_test()`), or, for ordinal
ratings from many raters, by the model-based kappa of @nelson2015
(`ord_kappa_test()`). For example, with 4 raters on a 5-point scale:

```{r}
ratings <- data.frame(
  Rater1 = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 4, 1, 2, NA, NA, NA),
  Rater2 = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2, 4, 1, 2, 5, NA, NA),
  Rater3 = c(NA, 3, 3, 3, 2, 3, 4, 2, 2, 5, 1, 3),
  Rater4 = c(1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 4, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, NA))
cac_test(col.names = c("Rater1", "Rater2", "Rater3", "Rater4"),
         data = ratings, weights = "quadratic")
```

See `vignette("categorical_agreement", package = "SimplyAgree")` for how
to choose a coefficient, weights for ordinal scales, the model-based kappa,
and comparisons between groups of raters or subjects.
